title: Safety planning and transitions of care
blurb: Write a collaborative safety plan, make means safer, and hand people over safely at discharge with timely follow-up and crisis options.
question: Mr Patel, 44, is leaving an acute ward tomorrow after a suicide attempt. His safety plan lists only his care coordinator's office number (9am to 5pm). He says his worst moments are late at night. What should the nurse change before discharge?

teach.body: A safety plan is a short, personal, written plan the person develops with staff (and family or carers where appropriate) for getting through a crisis: recognising their warning signs, using their own coping strategies, reaching people and services, and making their surroundings safer. NICE NG225 says it uses a problem-solving approach, is held by the person and is shared as they decide. In plain English: their own step-by-step guide for the worst moments, in their own words.

teach.h: The parts of a safety plan (NG225 1.11.7)

steps.label: Triggers and warning signs
steps.sub: Of rising distress, self-harm or suicidal crisis

steps.label: My coping strategies
steps.sub: Things I can do myself; barriers solved

steps.label: People who can help
steps.sub: Family or friends to support or resolve the crisis

steps.label: Services
steps.sub: MH team, out-of-hours and emergency contacts

steps.label: Safer environment
steps.sub: Remove or restrict lethal means together

teach.h: A good plan vs a weak plan

rows.label: Written by
values: The person with staff and family

teach.body: Reducing access to lethal means is one of the most direct ways to keep someone safe. NG225 asks professionals to establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them through therapeutic collaboration or negotiation. In prescribing, consider toxicity and agree smaller supplies (for example weekly). On wards, ligature risks are assessed because most suicides on the ward are by hanging or strangulation.

items.label: Assess needs incl. suicide risk; tell carers the date early
Care plan to all within 24 h; GP letter emailed within 24 h
Discharge summary within a week; GP appointment within 2 weeks

teach.h: What the discharge care plan includes (NG53 1.5.20)
head: Section
Examples
rows: Early warning signs agreed with the person
Who to contact and where to go
Date the plan will be reviewed

children.edge: Can be safely supported at home
children.label: Crisis resolution and home treatment

teach.body: Nurse Ofori sits with Mr Patel and rewrites the plan in his words. His warning signs are lying awake at 2am replaying the debt letters. His coping steps are a shower, a podcast and texting his brother, who has agreed to be called at night. They add the crisis line and out-of-hours team numbers. His stockpiled tablets are returned to the pharmacy and new medicines are dispensed weekly. Because suicide risk is identified, the community team will see him within 48 hours.

teach.text: A safety plan is not a 'no-suicide contract'. Asking someone to sign a promise not to harm themselves is not one of the NG225 components and does not make anyone safer. And a plan that only works in office hours fails at the times people are most at risk.

items: Safety plan: warning signs, own coping, people and places, helpers, services incl. out-of-hours, safer environment.
Written with the person (and family where appropriate), in their words, held by them, shared as they decide.
Make means safer collaboratively: medicines in smaller supplies, weapons, ligatures.
NG53: GP letter within 24 h; follow-up within 7 days, or 48 h if suicide risk identified.
Crisis resolution and home treatment teams support acute crises at home where safe.

summary: You can now build a collaborative safety plan with the NG225 components and agree safer access to means. You can also plan discharge so that follow-up, communication and crisis support arrive on time under NICE NG53.

A.q: Under NICE NG225, who should hold a person's safety plan?
options: The person themselves
The care coordinator's office
The GP practice record
The ward's crisis folder
A.why: NG225 1.11.8: the safety plan should be held by the person and shared with family, carers and professionals as the person decides.

whyNot.1: Staff may have copies, but the plan is held by the person.
whyNot.2: The GP may receive it if the person agrees; it is not held there.
whyNot.3: A ward folder is not accessible to the person in a crisis at home.

A.q: Under NICE NG53, within what time should a discharge letter be emailed to the GP after mental health in-patient discharge?
options: Within 7 days
Within 48 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 2 weeks
A.why: NG53 1.6.3: within 24 hours, a discharge letter is emailed to the GP; a fuller discharge summary follows within a week.

whyNot.0: Seven days is the follow-up standard and the discharge summary timeframe.
whyNot.1: 48 hours is the follow-up time where suicide risk is identified.
whyNot.3: Two weeks relates to considering a GP appointment.

A.q: Which item does NICE NG225 list as part of a safety plan?
options: A signed promise not to self-harm
A risk score for the next 7 days
Out-of-hours and emergency contacts
A list of medicines that are banned
A.why: NG225 1.11.7: include contact details for the mental health service, including out-of-hours and emergency contacts.

whyNot.0: A no-harm promise is not one of the NG225 safety plan components.
whyNot.1: NG225 advises against using risk scores to predict self-harm or suicide.
whyNot.3: Means safety is agreed collaboratively, not presented as banned lists.

B.q: While developing a safety plan, Mr Reed, 52, a farmer, says he keeps two shotguns at home. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Record it and review at his next appointment
Discuss with him how to make the guns safe
Tell him he must hand them to police today
Leave it out, as he holds a valid licence
B.why: NG225 1.7.1 and 1.11.7: establish the means and, if accessible, discuss removing or restricting them through therapeutic collaboration, recording the agreed plan.

whyNot.0: Delaying leaves highly lethal means available.
whyNot.2: Ordering rather than collaborating may damage engagement; the aim is an agreed plan.
whyNot.3: A licence does not reduce the risk of lethal means in a crisis.

B.q: Ms Ali, 20, wants her sister and her care team to have copies of her safety plan, but not her father. What should the nurse do?
options: Share it with her father as next of kin
Keep it in her notes until her next review
Ask her to choose one person to share it with
Share it with her sister and the care team
B.why: NG225 1.11.8: the plan is shared with family, carers and professionals as decided by the person.

whyNot.0: Sharing against her wishes breaches confidentiality and her choice.
whyNot.1: Holding it back ignores her wish and the plan's purpose of being available in a crisis.
whyNot.2: She can share with whoever she chooses; there is no limit of one.

B.q: Ms Rae, 38, has suicidal thoughts after a bereavement but no plan. She wants to stay at home with her partner and is willing to accept daily support. Which service is most appropriate?
options: Crisis resolution and home treatment team
Admission to a psychiatric intensive care unit
A routine referral to NHS Talking Therapies
An outpatient appointment in 6 weeks
B.why: Crisis resolution and home treatment teams provide intensive support at home for people in acute crisis where this is safe, the least restrictive option. NICE recommends considering CRHT for people at significant risk of suicide (NG222 1.16.10, more severe depression) and as first line for acute psychosis (CG178 1.4.1.1).

whyNot.1: PICU is for people who cannot be safely managed on an open ward.
whyNot.2: A routine referral is too slow and not crisis care.
whyNot.3: Six weeks leaves her unsupported during a crisis.

C.q: Mr Patel, 44, is leaving hospital after a suicide attempt. His plan lists his care coordinator's 9am to 5pm number, but he says the worst moments come at night. What is the priority change?
options: Add his GP practice's routine appointment line
Add out-of-hours crisis and emergency contacts
Advise him to wait until 9am to call the team
Delay discharge until nights are settled
C.why: NG225 1.11.7: the safety plan includes out-of-hours and emergency contacts. A plan that only works in office hours fails at his highest-risk times.

whyNot.0: A routine GP line is not available at night.
whyNot.2: Waiting for office hours leaves him without help in a crisis.
whyNot.3: Delaying discharge is not the answer to a fixable gap in the plan.

C.q: Mrs Shah, 66, is to be discharged from a mental health ward to live with her husband, her main carer. Which action best follows NICE NG53?
options: Phone him on the day of discharge
Assume his circumstances are unchanged
Send him the discharge summary in a week
Involve him and tell him the date early
C.why: NG53 1.5.22-1.5.23: recognise carers' circumstances may have changed, discuss progress with them and make sure they know the likely discharge date well in advance.

whyNot.0: Same-day notice does not let him prepare.
whyNot.1: NG53 asks staff to recognise that carers' circumstances may have changed.
whyNot.2: The summary is for professionals; carers need involvement before discharge.

C.q: Ms Ford, 27, is leaving an acute ward. Which content is essential in the care plan sent to everyone supporting her, according to NICE NG53?
options: Her relapse signs and where to go in a crisis
Her full risk score history from admission
A list of the ward staff who cared for her
Her nearest relative's financial details
C.why: NG53 1.5.20: the care plan should include possible relapse signs, who to contact and where to go in a crisis, among other items.

whyNot.1: Risk score histories are not part of the NG53 care plan content and do not guide crisis care.
whyNot.2: Ward staff names are not a listed care plan item.
whyNot.3: Relatives' finances are not part of her care plan.

reteach.title: Their plan, their words, any hour
reteach.question: What makes a safety plan work?

blocks.body: A safety plan works when the person wrote it with you, it uses their own words and warning signs, it lists things they can actually do and people they will actually call, it includes out-of-hours numbers, and dangerous means have been made safer together. Discharge then hands this plan on, with follow-up inside 48 hours if suicide risk is identified.

blocks.text: A 'no-harm contract' is not a safety plan.

explain.body: NG225: means of self-harm; triggers and warning signs; individual coping strategies; social contacts and settings for distraction; family or friends to help; service contacts including out-of-hours; keeping the environment safe.

test.q: Which of these does NICE NG225 list as a purpose of a safety plan?
options: Signing a safety contract with the team
Monitoring adherence to prescribed medicines
Recognising triggers and warning signs
Rating today's suicide risk level
test.why: NG225 1.11.7: safety plans are used to recognise the triggers and warning signs of increased distress, further self-harm or a suicidal crisis, alongside coping strategies, contacts and safer means.

whyNot.0: A no-harm contract is not one of the NG225 1.11.7 components.
whyNot.1: Medicines adherence is not an NG225 1.11.7 purpose; the plan addresses access to lethal means, not adherence.
whyNot.3: NG225 1.6.1-1.6.4: risk ratings are not used to predict suicide or decide care.

explain.body: Developed in collaboration with family and carers as appropriate, using a problem-solving approach, held by the person, shared as they decide, and accessible to them and professionals at times of crisis.

test.q: Which approach does NICE NG225 say a safety plan should use?
options: A problem-solving approach
A risk prediction approach
A behavioural contract approach
A standard ward template, unchanged
test.why: NG225 1.11.8: the safety plan should use a problem-solving approach and be developed collaboratively.

whyNot.2: Contracts are not the NG225 approach.
whyNot.3: An unchanged template is not personalised or collaborative.

explain.body: Establish the means and, if accessible, discuss removing them collaboratively. Consider medicine toxicity, agree smaller supplies such as weekly prescriptions, and ask for unwanted medicines to be returned.

test.q: A woman with recent overdoses is prescribed an antidepressant. Which approach best reduces access to means under NICE NG225?
options: A 3-month supply to improve adherence
Weekly supplies agreed with her
Switching to a tricyclic antidepressant
Asking her partner to hide all medicines
test.why: NG225 1.13.2: use shared decision-making to discuss limiting quantities, for example weekly prescriptions.

whyNot.2: Tricyclics are more toxic in overdose.
whyNot.3: Covert arrangements are not collaborative and may not be agreed by her.

explain.body: NG53: assess needs including suicide risk before discharge, involve carers early, send the GP letter within 24 hours, follow up within 7 days, or within 48 hours if suicide risk is identified.

test.q: A man with no identified suicide risk is discharged from a mental health ward. By when should he be followed up under NICE NG53?
options: Within 48 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 14 days
Within 7 days
test.why: NG53 1.6.7: follow up a person who has been discharged within 7 days; 48 hours applies if suicide risk is identified (1.6.8).

whyNot.0: 48 hours applies where suicide risk is identified.
whyNot.1: 24 hours is the GP letter deadline.
whyNot.2: 14 days is longer than the NG53 standard.
